docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
I am a graduate student pursuing a dual Master's degree in Mechanical Engineering (MechE) and Computional Science and Engineering (CSE) at MIT, currently working under the guidance of Prof. Pierre Lermusiaux in the MSEAS Research Group.

My interests lie at the intersection of the fields of (1) applied mathematics, (2) computational sciences and (3) fluid mechanics. My projects and research work throughout my engineering career has had a good balance of these components. My current work in graduate school involves two main topics: (1) the development of schemes for optimal path planning of autonomous marine vehicles and (2) numerical modeling of acoustic propagation in uncertain environments. Prior to joining MIT, I studied at McGill University where my undergraduate research delved into the field of aerodynamic shape optimization.

I am interested in using my unique background and experiences to tackle complicated problems and help solve some of the pressing issues that face our world today.

Additionally, I am an avid sports fan who enjoys both watching and playing basketball, soccer and tennis. I also play the tabla (a pair of hand drums used in Indian music) and love to travel and try out new cuisines.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text:
This section contains some of my class and personal projects that fall under the following broad fields:

  1. Uncertainty Quantification and Inference
  2. Machine Learning
  3. Numerical Methods and Numerical Differential Equations.

docs.title: Data Assimilative Path Planning
docs.text:
A key challenge in path planning for autonomous underwater and surface vehicles is navigating in ocean environments that are highly uncertain. Users will rarely have accurate information and forecasts of ocean currents and velocity fields (which have a non-negligible influence on the vehicle). As part of the class 16.S498 (Risk Aware and Robust Nonlinear Planning), I investigated (in a team of two) the task of path planning in these uncertain environments and how to incorporate data assimilation into the general path planning framework. By using measurements collected by the vehicle, we looked at how (using Bayesian filtering) this data could be used to reduce the overall uncertainty in the environment as well as update the vehicle path to allow for it to navigate both safely and quickly to the target.

The figure above shows a sample result from the proposed algorithm for a simple case of navigating in an uncertain flow field parametrized by a single random variable. Left subfigure: The possible paths taken by the vehicle for a fixed sequence of controls over short time intervals results in large uncertainty at the beginning which progressively collapses as environmental uncertainty is reduced from measurements and collected data. Right subfigure: The evolution of the pdf of the random flow variable (as desired, we converge to the true value as more data is collected).

Check out the full project report at this link -->

docs.title: Variational Methods for Bayesian Inference
docs.text:
A central task in Bayesian inference is the ability to accurately approximate and sample from the posterior distribution. As part of the class 16.940 (Numerical Methods for Stochastic Modeling and Inference) I looked at investigating one such family of methods that performs this task: variational methods. Variational inference reformulates the problem of approximating or sampling from the posterior as a deterministic optimization problem. The optimization is in general framed as finding a simpler distribution within a given family of densities (for example the exponential family) that best approximates the target distribution. In this project, we investigated two variational approaches, each falling in distinct categories: Stein variational methods for inference (a non-parametric approach) and mean-field variational inference (a parametric approach).

The figure above shows a sample result from this project for when the same posterior distribution is approximated using each approach. Stein's method (top row) uses a set of particles that are optimally moved to represent the posterior whereas the mean-field approach (bottom row) optimizes the hyperparameters of some candidate distribution belonging to some predefined family of densities.

Check out the full project report at this link -->

docs.title: Machine Learning and Statistical Learning Theory
Residual RNN Architectures Based on ODE Stability Theory
docs.text: The interpretation of deep learning architectures as time integration schemes and flow maps for dynamical systems has garnered much attention in recent years and led to numerous advancements ranging from Neural Ordinary Differential Equations to novel network architectures based on established time integration schemes (such as Runge-Kutta and Leap-frog methods). In this project, we aimed to follow along this trend to motivate the design of recurrent neural networks (RNNs). In particular, we looked at using the stability theory of ODEs and dynamical systems to investigate a new RNN architecture that aims to tackle two big issues in typical recurrent networks: (1) vanishing/exploding gradients and (2) robustness to input noise. We are currently working to convert this project into a paper, and will provide the link to that given paper for further details once it has been completed.

docs.title: The Adaptive Finite Element Method
docs.text:
A topic that I have always found to be really fascinating is that of adaptive mesh refinement, where the solver can automatically determine what parts of the domain the solution error is high and accordingly refine the mesh locally there. As part of the class 2.097 (Numerical Methods for PDEs) I decided to look into adaptive methods in detail by considering the h-adaptive finite element method. This project entailed coding from scratch (1) a continuous Galerkin solver on unstructured domains, (2) the error approximation scheme used to inform where to refine the mesh (based on the work of Babuska et al.) and (3) the mesh refinement algorithm for splitting elements while maintaining appropriate mesh quality. The figure above shows a sample result from the final code which was able to appropriately refine the mesh most in the top right corner of the domain to adequately resolve the numerical solution.

Check out the full project report at this link -->

Check out the code on Github at this link -->

docs.title: Acceleration Techniques for Restarted GMRES
docs.text:
GMRES has become a very popular algorithm in industry applications for iteratively solving nonsymmetric systems of linear equations. A key issue however is that, due to computer memory constraints, the algorithm typically requires to be "restarted" every few iterations (the best guess for the linear system's solution at the end of one restart cycle ends up being the initial guess for the next restart cycle and the process continues until convergence).

This restarting process can unfortunately weaken the convergence rate of the overall algorithm. As part of the class 18.335 (Numerical Linear Algebra), I therefore looked into acceleration techniques for restarted GMRES that aims to address this issue. In particular, I implemented and investigated the GMRES-E and LGMRES algorithms in Python and compared them to standard GMRES for some canonical test problems (sample convergence results are shown in the figure above).

Check out the full project report at this link -->

Check out the code on Github at this link -->

docs.title: Time-Optimal Path Planning under Harvesting Constraints
docs.text:
Path planning for autonomous surface and underwater vehicles has gained plenty of attention in the past few decades. Our research has involved how to generate time optimal paths under constraints where the vehicle must harvest some specified amount of a field from the environment (ex. energy, marine plastic pollution, etc.) before reaching the target. Our PDE based approach is moreover able to obtain globally optimal solutions to this path planning problem.

Read more at this link -->

docs.title: Acoustic Modeling in Uncertain Environments
docs.text:
Since electromagnetic waves get attenuated in water, the only way to communicate and navigate underwater is through acoustic means. Due to this, the need for accurate models for acoustic propagation is crucial for marine applications. What makes things even more challenging is that the ocean environment is highly uncertain and so a useful acoustic model must inherently account for this randomness. Motivated by this fact, this project involves the problem of modeling high frequency acoustic propagation in ocean environments that are uncertain. This uncertainty can arise from numerous areas including the sound speed profile and acoustic source location. Our approach has looked into acoustic wavefront propagation using level set methods. To quantify the uncertainty in the acoustic wavefront after propagating through the unknown ocean environment, we have been using a reduced order method known as the Dynamically Orthogonal (DO) equations. We are further looking at how we may use these predictions along with measurements to perform acoustic Bayesian inference.

The figure above shows a sample result from our level set approach when propagating an acoustic wavefront in a deterministic environment. To allow for the wavefront to intersect and pass through itself, we look to represent it in an augmented phase space as the intersection of two level sets (left-most subfigure). The resulting wavefront's propagation in the actual physical domain (given here by a channel with a curved bottom) is shown in the right-most subfigure.

docs.title: Adjoint Based Aerodynamic Shape Optimization for High Order Methods
docs.text:
High order methods are being studied increasingly as approaches for numerically simulating flows as they allow for much higher accuracy as compared to traditional finite volume CFD solvers. This research project looked at joining adjoint based optimization (an efficient method for gradient based optimization) with these high order methods in order to tackle aerospace design problems.

Read more at this link -->

docs.title: Free Form Deformation for Aerodynamic Shape Optimization
docs.text:
A big challenge in aerodynamic shape optimization is figuring out how to represent the object of interest so that it can be optimized easily (this task is called shape parametrization). For example, if a wing were to be optimized, one approach is to discretely represent the wing surface using lots of triangles (ex. using Delaunay triangulation) and then consider the vertices of these triangles as the degrees of freedom. The issue of course is that such an option can result in thousands, if not millions, of design parameters in the optimization problem (making it too expensive to solve) and it could also result in shapes that aren't sufficiently smooth.

This project is one that I looked into during the summer of my sophomore year on a shape parametrization approach known as Free Form Deformation (FFD). Originating from computer graphics, FFD looks to build a lattice of points around an object of interest. These points can then be moved to deform the shape it encloses. The lattice allows for a much smaller number of degrees of freedom for the optimization problem and it also allows for the easy generation of smooth candidate shapes. This project involved looking into how to create tight fitting FFD boxes around arbitrarily shaped objects as well as how to create combinations of inter-connected FFD boxes that would allow for better local shape control while maintaining surface continuity requirements. The figure above shows some sample results of a wing's deformation using an FFD lattice.

At the end of the summer, we were invited to give a talk to Bombardier Aerospace's Advanced Aerodynamics Group on the applicability of FFD in aerospace design problems. The slides for this talk can be found at this link.

docs.title: Adjoint Based Aerodynamic Shape Optimization for High Order Methods
docs.text: Collaborators: Philip Zwanenburg and Prof. Siva Nadarajah

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Fig.1 - A schematic showing where the inaccuracies in representing shapes arise when transitioning between CAD software and Analysis (ex. CFD) and/or optimization software. CAD software represents the airfoil using NURBS basis functions resulting in the blue shapes. Analysis and optimization software instead represent shapes typically using polynomials resulting in the orange shapes. Transitioning between the two different function spaces results in inaccuracies.

A major bottleneck in the traditional aerodynamic shape optimization design process today is in interfacing with Computer Aided Design (CAD) software. CAD software will typically represent its objects and shapes using what are known as NURBS basis functions. On the other hand, analysis software (for instance computational fluid dynamics (CFD) software) and optimization programs (which will typically also be included in the same CFD software) traditionally use polynomial basis functions to represent shapes and boundaries. This discrepancy results in some key challenges and loss of accuracy. Specifically, when transitioning from the CAD software to the CFD/optimization software, we have to approximate the NURBS geometric model using polynomials and this results in inaccuracies in representing the original shape. Once the model has been analyzed and optimized, we have to once again transition the object back to the CAD software so that it can be integrated with the larger design, placed into manufacturing drawings, etc. Due to the same discrepancies in shape parameterization, this step once again requires an approximation to the shape and results in its inexact representation (the above schematic visually shows how these issues arise in each step). Addressing these inaccuracies in shape parametrization is ultimately an important and relevant problem, and is needed to close this gap between CAD and analysis/optimization software in the typical engineering design cycle.

docs.title: Our Research
docs.text:
This project looked to address this issue and discrepancy in shape parametrization through looking at the NURBS-Enhanced Discontinuous Galerkin Method. At a high level, this is simply a numerical method that can be used in CFD applications for simulating fluid flows. It brings together two different approaches: (1) The NURBS-Enhanced Approach and (2) The Discontinuous Galerkin (DG) method:

  • The Discontinuous Galerkin method falls in the class of what are known as high-order methods for numerically solving PDEs. Compared to standard Finite Volume methods, DG methods differ in that they are able to allow for the numerical solution to the PDE to be solved with much higher accuracy.

  • The NURBS-Enhanced part effectively augments the standard DG method by allowing for shapes that are represented using NURBS basis functions (as is done in CAD software) to be represented exactly in the DG solver. In this way, we are able to close the gap and remove the shape inaccuracy errors when transitioning from the CAD to the CFD solver.

As we were further interested in optimizing the shape for aerodynamic efficiency (ex. to minimize drag, maximize lift, etc.) this project looked additionally at merging adjoint based optimization with the NURBS-Enhanced DG solver. The adjoint method, at a high level, allows for a quick an efficient way to obtain the gradient of the cost function being minimized in the optimization problem (ex. drag) with respect to the parameters used to represent the shape. With these gradients in hand, any nonlinear gradient based optimization approach (ex. Sequential Quadratic Programming) can then be used to optimize the resulting shape (Fig. 2).

Fig.2 - The standard workflow for adjoint-based shape optimization.

Our ultimate research goal was to demonstrate adjoint based aerodynamic shape optimization for the NURBS-Enhanced Discontinuous Galerkin (DG) method. Although our results were preliminary, they show promise for one approach to tackle the challenges with shape parametrization when transitioning between CAD and CFD software.

docs.title: Sample Results - Symmetric Airfoil Optimization
docs.text:
Fig.3 - The unstructured mesh around the initial, unoptimized airfoil.

We show here sample results from our developed method for the problem of optimizing a symmetric airfoil in 2D. We consider in particular the problem of optimizing the airfoil to attain a target lift coefficient of 0.25 while constraining the pitching moment to have a value of -0.1255.

Fig.4 - (Top) The initial and optimized airfoil profiles. (Bottom left) The convergence in the lift coefficient as a function of design iteration for each airfoil. (Bottom right) The drop in the cost function (the function we are minimizing in the optimization problem) vs. design iterations.

The optimized airfoil as well as the progression in the cost function and lift coefficient as a function of design iteration are shown in the above figure. We see that the trailing edge is slightly modified to give the airfoil the desired target lift while satisfying the pitching moment constraint. In these figures, there are several values of "P" reported as well. This corresponds to the accuracy of the NURBS-Enhanced DG solver used to simulate the flow. A higher value of "P" essentially results in a higher accuracy solver being used.

docs.title: Time-Optimal Path Planning under Harvesting Constraints
docs.text: Collaborators: Manan Doshi and Prof. Pierre Lermusiaux

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Fig.1 - Left: A solar powered AUV that could be used in energy optimal path planning. Right: The great pacific garbage patch, an example where optimal marine plastic cleanup could be applicable.

The past decades have seen a growing use of sea surface craft (sailboats, vessels, ships) and autonomous vehicles (propelled AUVs, ocean gliders, solar-vehicles, etc.) in marine applications ranging from military surveillance to scientific data collection. Central to the effective operation of all autonomous surface and underwater vehicles is efficient and accurate motion control which falls under the purview of path planning. Path planning, in the most general sense, corresponds to a set of rules to be provided to an autonomous robot for navigating from one configuration to another in some optimal fashion. The metric for optimality, moreover, is problem dependent and depends on the user specified objective of interest and can include minimizing travel time, minimizing energy use or maximizing vehicle safety.

Increasingly, having autonomous vehicles collect/harvest external fields from the environment has grown in relevance. The applications in which this is important are numerous. For instance, in the case of energy optimal path planning where long endurance and low power are crucial, it is important to be able to optimally harvest energy (ex. solar energy) along the way and/or leverage the environment (ex. the velocity field and currents) to reduce energy expenditure. This idea of optimal field collection extends further than just energy and is applicable to problems such as path planning to optimally collect marine plastic pollution or oil spills as well.

Our research goal has thus been simple: to derive exact time-optimal control equations that optimally account for harvesting environmental fields.

docs.title: Our Research
docs.text:
Fig.2 - The general problem description (note that energy has been used as the harvesting field but the choice of field to collect is completely arbitrary in our framework)

The figure above describes the key parameters involved in the problem that we aim to solve (the figure involves the case of energy collection but it is important to note that our methodology is equally applicable to harvest other types of fields (plastic, oil, etc.)). Our goal is to be able to optimally navigate a vehicle from a specified start point to a destination in minimal time under the constraint of having collected a specified minimum amount of the external field. Navigating in this environment is not simple as we must account for, first, the external velocity field (which may be dynamic) in which the vehicle is being advected. Second, we have to account for harvesting from the background field, which also may be dynamic!

Using principles from optimal control theory, we have been able to derive PDE based schemes that account for harvesting as a constraint in the path planning process. The solutions obtained from our schemes are moreover globally optimal. The following case shows an example of some the types of problems that we have been able to solve using our approach.

docs.title: Sample Case - Time Optimal Path Planning with Energy Constraints
docs.text:
Fig.3 - The external environment for the case of interest. Left: The energy input field, which is static. Right: The external velocity field along with the start point and moving target (star).

This case considers the problem of path planning under energy constraints. We consider the situation where the autonomous vehicle travels at its fixed maximum speed but has freedom to control its heading when navigating. From a given start point, we must additionally plan a path in a highly dynamic flow field to intercept a moving target point (right subfigure in Fig.3). We can further harvest energy from some static input energy field (ex. a solar input field) and the input flux distribution is shown in the left subfigure of Fig. 3. The vehicle starts with 0.325 units of energy and it must reach the target with at least 0.6 units of energy in a minimal amount of time. Note also that since the vehicle speed is constant, its energy expenditure rate is assumed to be a fixed constant in this problem.

Fig.4 - Left: The optimal path for the vehicle to take for this case. Right: The evolution of the energy of the vehicle as its traverses to the target.

Fig. 4 shows the optimal path as returned from our approach for this problem at hand. We see that the vehicle stays as much as it can in regions with high energy input flux and it uses the external flow field to its advantage in order to reach the target quickly. It is important to reiterate that our PDE based scheme is able to find the global optimal solution to this path planning problem. No other path exists that can reach the target in less time while also having 0.6 units of energy when reaching the target.

docs.title: Challenges and Next Steps
docs.text: We are further working on augmenting our schemes through various further steps. One such avenue is accounting for uncertainty in the path planning framework. In many cases, the external velocity field is uncertain and the harvesting field as well may be random. We are therefore looking at how to generate optimal paths in these environments with appropriate probabilistic bounds.
